cases.title: Gray or Red?
cases.presentation: Tanker explosion. 40+ casualties, 4 ambulances on scene, 15 min to the next wave. A man with ~90% full-thickness burns is breathing shallowly, unresponsive, weak pulse.
cases.question: SALT category now?
options: D: EXPECTANT — survival unlikely with current resources; comfort care and re-triage when resources improve.
cases.explanation: SALT's Expectant category exists for this scenario. Resources spent on him now cost several salvageable lives. Provide analgesia/comfort and re-triage as resources arrive.
cases.clinicalPearl: Gray is 'not now', not 'never' — re-triage when the scene changes.

cases.title: The Lost Tourniquet Time
cases.presentation: At the hospital, a red patient arrives with a tourniquet on his thigh. No tag notes, no time. Nobody on scene remembers when it went on.
cases.question: What scene practice would have prevented this?
options: B: Writing 'TQ + time' on the tag (and/or forehead) at application.
C: Telling the patient to remember.
D: Not applying tourniquets in MCIs.
cases.explanation: Tourniquet time drives surgical decision-making. The tag is the record that travels with the patient.
cases.clinicalPearl: TQ without a time is half a treatment.

cases.title: Red Area Overflowing
cases.presentation: Your treatment area has 22 'red' patients and 3 yellows from a nightclub stampede. Transport is stalled. On re-triage, 12 of the reds are alert, have good pulses, no respiratory distress, and minor injuries.
cases.question: What happened and what now?
options: A: Transport in order of arrival.
B: Nothing — better safe than sorry.
C: Over-triage is clogging the red area and transport; re-triage and re-tag downward so true reds move first.
D: Request 22 more ambulances and keep tags.
cases.explanation: Over-triage buries true reds and wastes transport. Re-triage corrects it — that's the system working.
